428.title: The Gosinga grove
428.hook: which monk would light up the grove? each answers from his own practice
428.howItsDone: Buddhist traditions honor many temperaments of practice, from study and teaching to forest asceticism and meditation, and MN 32 is often taught as a picture of a community where each kind of practitioner has a place.

segments.voice: Yesterday: milk and water, three friends who didn't keep score. Did you fill one empty jar for someone, quietly? Today we go back to the same wood, on a different night. Day four hundred twenty-eight.

It's a clear night with the moon full. The sal trees are in bloom, and the text says the whole wood smells as if heavenly scents were drifting through it. Six of the Buddha's great disciples have gathered in the Gosinga grove. Sariputta looks around and asks the others a question that sounds almost like a parlor game: what kind of monk would light up this grove? Everyone answers. Nobody gives the same answer. Today: the Gosinga grove.
screen: `A FULL MOON, THE SAL TREES IN BLOOM.` → `SIX GREAT DISCIPLES.` → `WHO WOULD LIGHT UP THIS GROVE?`

segments.voice: This is the thirty-second discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings, the greater discourse in Gosinga. Listen to the answers. Ananda, who memorized the teachings, says: a monk who has learned much and remembers it, and teaches it clearly. Revata says: a monk who delights in solitary meditation. Anuruddha, known for his inner sight, says: a monk who sees a thousand worlds with the divine eye. Mahakassapa, the strict forest monk, says: one who lives in the forest, eats only alms food, wears rag robes, wants little, and praises those things to others. Moggallana says: two monks discussing the teaching deeply, asking and answering without faltering. And Sariputta says: a monk who masters his own mind, who can rest in whatever state he chooses in the morning, at noon or at evening, like a king with a chest full of clothes who wears whatever color he likes. Do you hear it? Each one names his own practice. That's not vanity. It's honesty. You can only praise what you actually love. Then they go to the Buddha and ask: who spoke best? And he says: all of you spoke well, each in your own way. Then he gives his own answer: a monk who sits down after his meal, legs crossed, body straight, determined not to get up until his mind is free. The Buddha doesn't rank them. A community is lit by many lamps, and the light is different from each one. The learner, the hermit, the seer, the ascetic, the debater, the master of mind. One grove.
screen: `SIX ANSWERS UNDER A FULL MOON` · `EACH NAMES THE PRACTICE HE LOVES` · `ALL OF YOU SPOKE WELL` · `THE BUDDHA: SIT UNTIL THE MIND IS FREE` · then, large: `EACH LIGHTS IT DIFFERENTLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say what lights your grove. Sit, and ask yourself Sariputta's question. Not what should light it, but what actually does, for you. Is it learning something and understanding it? Quiet time alone? Wanting less? A good conversation? Steadying your mind? Let one answer come. Don't argue with it. Then sit for the rest of the time the way the Buddha described: body straight, settled, simply here. The bell holds the time.
The Gosinga grove. A wood of blooming sal trees, a full moon, and six disciples who each light it in their own way. Today's word.
Your line: each lights it differently. Today, notice one person whose way of practicing or working isn't yours, and name to yourself the light they bring. Day four hundred twenty-eight.

match.prompt: who lights the grove how — tap the pairs.
pairs: learned much, and teaches it clearly
forest, alms food, rag robes, few wants
masters his mind, like a king's wardrobe

myth: the Buddha chose one answer as the best
he said all of them spoke well, each in their own way, and then gave his own.
each disciple named the practice he himself was known for
Ananda praised learning, Revata solitude, Anuruddha the divine eye, and so on.
the conversation happened on a moonlit night with sal trees in bloom
the text sets it in the Gosinga wood on a clear night, the trees flowering.

fork.setup: six disciples come to you, each with a different answer to the question 'who would light up this grove?' they ask which one is best. you're the Buddha. what do you say?
options: Sariputta's; he's the wisest.
all of you spoke well, each in your own way.
none of you; only I light the grove.
fork.reveal: the Buddha affirms every answer, and then adds his own: a monk who sits determined not to rise until his mind is free.

original.note: Pali gosinga: cow's horn (go, cow + singa, horn), the name of the sal-tree wood.

trapdoor: what you thought: there's one right way to be a good practitioner.
what it means: a community is lit by many kinds of practice, each honest about what it loves.
what a scholar hears: MN 32's answers match each disciple's title elsewhere in the canon, such as Anuruddha foremost in the divine eye and Mahakassapa in ascetic practices (AN 1).

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 32, Mahagosinga Sutta (the greater discourse in Gosinga)

429.title: The cowherd's skills
429.hook: eleven skills of a good cowherd, and of a good monk
429.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often draw on farming and herding similes like MN 33 to present practice as a set of learnable skills: restraint of the senses, removing harmful thoughts, asking those more learned, moderation in what one accepts, and respect for elders.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Gosinga grove, and your line, each lights it differently. Did you notice someone whose light isn't yours? Day four hundred twenty-nine.

Ask a farmer what makes a good herder, and you won't hear about love of animals or a sense of calling. You'll hear about flies. Wounds. Which field still has grass in August. Whether you know your own cows by sight. Farming is a craft of small, boring, crucial skills. The Buddha grew up in farming country, and once he listed eleven of those skills, one by one, and then showed that each was also a skill of the spiritual life. Today: the cowherd's skills.
screen: `ASK A FARMER: NOT LOVE, BUT FLIES.` → `SMALL, BORING, CRUCIAL SKILLS.` → `ELEVEN OF THEM, ONE BY ONE.`

segments.voice: This is the thirty-third discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings, the greater discourse on the cowherd. A good cowherd knows the shape of his cattle and knows their markings. He picks the flies' eggs out of their hides. He dresses their wounds. He makes smoke to drive the insects off. He knows the watering place, and knows when they've had enough to drink. He knows the road, and he knows good pasture. He doesn't milk them dry, but leaves some for the calves. And he gives special care to the old bulls who lead the herd. Now the Buddha turns each one. Knowing the shape of the cattle is knowing the body: what it's made of. Knowing the markings is knowing that a fool and a wise person are marked by what they do. Picking out the flies' eggs is not letting thoughts of greed, ill will and cruelty settle in and hatch. Dressing the wounds is guarding the senses. Making smoke is teaching others what you've learned. The watering place is going to people who know more, and asking questions. Knowing when they've drunk is feeling the meaning land. The road is the eightfold path. The pasture is the four foundations of mindfulness. Not milking dry is accepting only what you need from people who give. And honoring the old bulls is kindness toward elders, in deed, word and thought. Notice how unglamorous these are. Not one is a vision or a miracle. Flies' eggs. Smoke. The spiritual life, here, is a craft, and crafts are learned one small skill at a time.
screen: `ELEVEN SKILLS OF A GOOD COWHERD` · `FLIES' EGGS: THOUGHTS THAT HATCH` · `THE PASTURE: THE FOUR MINDFULNESSES` · `A CRAFT, LEARNED SKILL BY SKILL` · then, large: `KNOW YOUR HERD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn one small skill. Today, take the flies' eggs. Sit, and watch the mind. When a sour thought lands, irritation, envy, a little cruelty, don't fight it and don't feed it. Notice it, the way a cowherd spots an egg on a hide, and gently brush it off by coming back to the breath. Do it again when the next one lands. That's the whole skill. The bell holds the time.
The cowherd's skills. Eleven plain crafts of tending a herd, each one a craft of tending a mind. Today's word.
Your line: know your herd. Today, pick one of the eleven, maybe the smoke, the watering place or the old bulls, and practice it once on purpose. Day four hundred twenty-nine.

match.prompt: the cowherd and the monk — tap the pairs.

myth: a good cowherd takes every drop of milk
he doesn't milk dry; he leaves some, as a monk accepts only what he needs from those who give.
the road, in the simile, is the eightfold path
and the pasture is the four foundations of mindfulness.
most of the eleven skills are about visions and miracles
they're plain crafts: flies' eggs, smoke, wounds, water and pasture.

fork.setup: you're a cowherd. you spot flies' eggs on a cow's hide. it's late, and you're tired. what does a good cowherd do?
options: leave them; they'll fall off.
pick them out now, before they hatch.
sell the cow.
fork.reveal: a good cowherd picks the eggs out. the Buddha's monk does the same with thoughts of greed, ill will and cruelty, before they settle in.

original.note: Pali gopalaka: cowherd (go, cow + palaka, keeper). the discourse is the Mahagopalaka Sutta.

trapdoor: what you thought: spiritual life is about big moments of insight.
what it means: it's a craft, built from small daily skills like a herder's.

what a scholar hears: the very next discourse, MN 34, keeps the herder: a foolish cowherd drives his cattle across the Ganges where there is no ford, and a wise one crosses at the ford, strongest bulls first.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 33, Mahagopalaka Sutta (the greater discourse on the cowherd)

430.title: Saccaka's boast
430.hook: a famous debater boasts he will shake the Buddha, and sweats instead
430.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers use MN 35's question, whether we can command the body and mind to be as we wish, as a classic way into the teaching of not-self (anatta) and the five aggregates.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the cowherd's skills, and your line, know your herd. Which of the eleven small skills did you try on purpose? Day four hundred thirty.

In the city of Vesali there lives a debater named Saccaka, and he is very good. He says so himself. He tells crowds there is no teacher alive who wouldn't shake and tremble if he debated them. Even a post, he says, would shake if he argued with it, never mind a human being. Then he hears what the Buddha teaches, and he announces he'll go and drag him around like a man dragging a sheep by its fleece. Five hundred people come to watch. Today: Saccaka's boast.
screen: `A DEBATER IN VESALI.` → `EVEN A POST WOULD SHAKE.` → `FIVE HUNDRED COME TO WATCH.`

segments.voice: This is the thirty-fifth discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings, the shorter discourse to Saccaka. Saccaka opens. He says the body is my self, feeling is my self, perception, mental formations, consciousness: all of these are my self. The Buddha doesn't argue back at once. He asks a question. A king rules his country. Can he have someone executed, fined or banished? Of course, says Saccaka. Then you say the body is your self. Can you command it: let my body be like this, don't let it be like that? Saccaka goes silent. The Buddha asks again. Silence again. The text adds a dramatic touch: a spirit named Vajirapani hovers above with a thunderbolt, and only Saccaka can see him. The Buddha asks a third time, and Saccaka answers: no. I can't command it. Then the same for feeling, perception, formations, consciousness. If it can't be commanded, and it changes, and it brings pain when it changes, is it fit to call it mine, I, my self? No. At the end, sweat pours from Saccaka's forehead, soaks through his robe and drips to the ground. The Buddha notes, gently, that there's no sweat on his own body. And one of the crowd says Saccaka looks like a crab with its legs broken, unable to crawl back into its pond. Here's the turn: Saccaka isn't a villain. He invites the Buddha and the monks to a meal the next day, and later he comes back for another talk, which we hear tomorrow. Certainty that has never been tested often sweats when it is.
screen: `THE BODY IS MY SELF, SAYS SACCAKA` · `A KING RULES; CAN YOU RULE YOUR BODY?` · `SILENCE, THEN NO` · `SWEAT ON HIS ROBE, NONE ON THE BUDDHA` · then, large: `THE SWEAT OF CERTAINTY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let one boast pass. Sit, and try the Buddha's question on yourself. Tell your body: don't let this knee ache, don't let my mind wander. Then watch what happens over the next minute. Notice the body and mind doing what they do, whether you command them or not. No sweat required. If a little thought of 'I'm good at this' shows up, let it pass too, like Saccaka's crowd going home. The bell holds the time.
Saccaka's boast. The debater who said even a post would shake before him, and ended up sweating, then coming back for more. Today's word.
Your line: the sweat of certainty. Today, when you feel very sure in an argument, ask yourself one honest question before you answer. Day four hundred thirty.

match.prompt: the debate in Vesali — tap the pairs.
pairs: even a post would shake before me
can't be commanded to be thus
how Saccaka looked at the end

myth: the Buddha won by out-arguing Saccaka point by point
he asked a question: can you command your body to be as you wish? Saccaka's silence did the rest.
Saccaka sweated through his robe while the Buddha didn't sweat
the text says Saccaka's sweat dripped to the ground, and the Buddha's body had none.
Saccaka left angry and never came back
he invited the Buddha to a meal, and returned for another conversation in MN 36.

fork.setup: you're Saccaka. the Buddha asks: can you command your body, 'let it be like this, not like that'? five hundred people are watching. what do you do?
options: insist yes, loudly.
stay silent.
change the subject to the weather.
fork.reveal: Saccaka stays silent twice. asked a third time, he admits: no. then the sweat starts.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about the Buddha winning a debate.
what it means: what changes, can't be commanded and brings pain isn't fit to be called 'mine, I, my self'.

what a scholar hears: Saccaka is called a son of the Niganthas (the Jain tradition) and an Aggivessana by clan, and his question-and-answer here closely follows the Buddha's second discourse on not-self (SN 22.59).

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 35, Culasaccaka Sutta (the shorter discourse to Saccaka)
Samyutta Nikaya 22.59, Anattalakkhana Sutta (the characteristic of not-self)

431.title: The greater Saccaka
431.hook: pleasant feeling does not invade his mind; the story of the austerities retold
431.howItsDone: Buddhists across traditions retell the austerities, the memory under the rose-apple tree and the bowl of rice as the turn toward the middle way; in meditation, many practice letting pleasant and painful feelings arise without being carried away by them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Saccaka's boast, and your line, the sweat of certainty. Did you ask yourself one honest question before answering? Today, Saccaka comes back. Day four hundred thirty-one.

It's morning in Vesali. The Buddha has dressed and taken his bowl to go for alms, and here comes Saccaka, walking up for another round. This time he's not boasting. He has a sharper question, almost a personal one. Some teachers train the body, he says, and some train the mind. Have you ever felt a pleasant feeling so strong it carried your mind away? Or a pain so strong it did? The Buddha answers with his own story. Today: the greater Saccaka.
screen: `SACCAKA COMES BACK.` → `HAS PLEASURE EVER CARRIED YOU AWAY?` → `THE BUDDHA TELLS HIS OWN STORY.`

segments.voice: This is the thirty-sixth discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings, and it holds the most vivid account of the Buddha's years of austerity anywhere in the early texts. He tells Saccaka he tried everything. He pressed his tongue to his palate and crushed his mind with his mind, until sweat ran from his armpits. He held his breath until his head felt split by a sharp sword, and his belly felt carved by a butcher's knife. He ate less and less, until his limbs looked like knotted vine stems, his spine stood out like a string of beads, his ribs like the rafters of a ruined shed, and his eyes sank like the gleam of water at the bottom of a deep well. And after each of these, he says the same strange line: the painful feeling that arose in me did not invade my mind and remain. He could bear it. But bearing it didn't free him. Then he remembered a day in childhood. His father was working in the fields, and he sat in the cool shade of a rose-apple tree, and his mind settled into a quiet, wholesome joy. He asked himself: why am I afraid of that kind of happiness, which has nothing to do with sense pleasures? I'm not afraid of it. So he ate some rice. The five companions left in disgust. And that night of practice led to awakening. And through all of it, he tells Saccaka, the pleasant feeling, too, did not invade my mind and remain. Not pain, not pleasure. Both came. Neither took over.
screen: `SACCAKA'S SHARPER QUESTION` · `THE AUSTERITIES, TOLD IN HIS OWN WORDS` · `THE ROSE-APPLE TREE, REMEMBERED` · `PAIN CAME, JOY CAME, NEITHER STAYED` · then, large: `IT DIDN'T INVADE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: feel pleasure without grasping. Find one pleasant thing in this moment: warmth in your hands, the chair holding you, the quiet. Let yourself enjoy it fully. Don't push it away. Then notice the little lean in the mind that says, more, keep this. Watch the pleasant feeling stay or fade on its own, while you stay where you are, enjoying it and not holding it. The bell holds the time.
The greater Saccaka. The long discourse where the Buddha tells of his austerities, the rose-apple tree, and a mind that pain and pleasure could visit but not take over. Today's word.
Your line: it didn't invade. Today, when something very pleasant or very unpleasant happens, let it be felt, and then say the line to see if it's true. Day four hundred thirty-one.

match.prompt: the austerities, in his words — tap the pairs.
pairs: like the rafters of a ruined shed
like water in a deep well
a childhood memory of quiet joy

myth: the austerities freed him because he could bear the pain
he could bear it: the pain didn't invade his mind. but bearing it didn't free him.
a childhood memory helped turn him toward the middle way
he remembered sitting in the shade of a rose-apple tree while his father worked, his mind quiet and glad.
his five companions approved when he ate rice
they left him in disgust, thinking he had given up.

fork.setup: you've fasted until your ribs show like rafters. you remember a day of quiet, wholesome joy under a tree as a child. you're afraid of that happiness. what do you decide?
options: fear it: any pleasure is a trap.
there's no need to fear a happiness that has nothing to do with sense pleasures.
go home to the palace.
fork.reveal: he asks why he's afraid of that happiness, and decides he isn't. he eats some rice, his companions walk out, and the path to awakening opens.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Buddha gave up the austerities because they were too hard.
what it means: he could endure them; they simply didn't lead to freedom, and a quiet joy remembered from childhood pointed another way.
what a scholar hears: MN 36's refrain, that pleasant and painful feeling 'did not invade the mind and remain', answers Saccaka's charge that the Buddha's followers train only the mind, not the body.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 36, Mahasaccaka Sutta (the greater discourse to Saccaka)

432.title: Shaking the palace
432.hook: Moggallana shakes the god Sakka's palace with his toe to wake him from pride
432.howItsDone: Many Buddhists know the phrase 'nothing is worth clinging to' from this discourse, and teachers often use the story of Moggallana and Sakka to show that even pleasant, heavenly lives can make people careless about practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the greater Saccaka, and your line, it didn't invade. When something strong came, pleasant or not, could you feel it without being taken over? Day four hundred thirty-two.

Sakka is king of the gods of the Thirty-Three, one of the heavens in Buddhist cosmology. One day he visits the Buddha and asks a big question in a few words: how is a monk freed by the ending of craving? The Buddha answers briefly. Sakka is delighted, bows, and goes home to heaven. Then the monk Moggallana, sitting nearby, starts to wonder. Did Sakka actually understand that, or did he just enjoy it? Today: shaking the palace.
screen: `SAKKA, KING OF THE GODS, ASKS.` → `A SHORT ANSWER. A HAPPY GOD.` → `DID HE UNDERSTAND IT?`

segments.voice: This is the thirty-seventh discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings, the shorter discourse on the ending of craving. The heart of the Buddha's answer is one short phrase: nothing is worth clinging to. A monk who has heard that knows everything directly, and whatever feeling comes, pleasant, painful or neither, he sees it as impermanent and lets it go. So Moggallana, known for his powers, travels to the heaven of the Thirty-Three to check. He finds Sakka in a garden, surrounded by heavenly music. Moggallana asks about the teaching, and Sakka brushes it aside: we gods are so busy. Instead, he shows off. Come and see my palace, the Vejayanta, built after our victory over the titans. Look at the towers. Look at the rooms. Even the goddesses peek out shyly at the visiting monk. Moggallana thinks: this god is living too carelessly. So he does something only he could do. With his big toe, the text says, he makes the whole palace shake and quake and tremble. Sakka and his court are amazed. Their pride goes quiet. Then Moggallana asks: what did the Buddha tell you, briefly, about the ending of craving? And this time Sakka repeats the teaching back, word for word. He had heard it the first time. He just couldn't hear it from inside the palace. Isn't that true for us too? A teaching can delight us and then slide right past us, because we go straight back to admiring our towers. Sometimes it takes a little shaking.
screen: `NOTHING IS WORTH CLINGING TO` · `MOGGALLANA VISITS THE HEAVEN` · `SAKKA SHOWS OFF HIS PALACE` · `A BIG TOE, AND THE PALACE TREMBLES` · then, large: `SHAKE THE PALACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: shake one assumption. Sit, and think of one thing you're quietly proud of and lean on: a skill, a title, a house, a reputation, being the reasonable one. Picture it as a palace with towers. Now, gently, like a toe tapping the floor, ask: is this worth clinging to? Don't answer quickly. Just feel the walls tremble a little. Then let the picture go and rest with the breath, which needs no palace. The bell holds the time.
Shaking the palace. Moggallana's toe on a god's floor: a little shock that wakes pride enough to hear the teaching. Today's word.
Your line: shake the palace. Today, when you catch yourself showing off, even inwardly, tap the floor lightly with one foot, and remember what's worth clinging to. Day four hundred thirty-two.

match.prompt: who did what in heaven — tap the pairs.
pairs: king of the gods of the Thirty-Three
shakes the palace with his toe

myth: Sakka had forgotten the teaching entirely
once the palace shook, he repeated it back word for word; he'd heard it, but pride drowned it out.
Moggallana went to heaven to check whether Sakka understood
he wondered whether the god had truly grasped it or only enjoyed it.
the palace was shaken by an earthquake
the text says Moggallana made it shake with his big toe.

fork.setup: you're Moggallana. you've come to check on a god who heard the Buddha teach, and instead he's giving you a tour of his palace. what do you do?
options: admire the palace politely and leave.
shake the palace, so his pride goes quiet.
lecture him for an hour.
fork.reveal: Moggallana shakes the palace with his toe. amazed and humbled, Sakka then repeats the Buddha's teaching back exactly.

original.note: Pali pasada: palace, mansion. Sakka's palace is the Vejayanta pasada.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about a monk with superpowers.
what it means: comfort and pride can make us deaf to what we've heard; a little shock can wake us up.
what a scholar hears: in Buddhist cosmology even gods like Sakka are not enlightened by being gods: they are beings in a pleasant birth, still subject to craving and to death.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 37, Culatanhasankhaya Sutta (the shorter discourse on the destruction of craving)

433.title: Sati's mistake
433.hook: a monk says the same consciousness wanders on unchanged; the Buddha: consciousness arises from conditions
433.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers use MN 38's fire simile to explain that consciousness arises dependent on conditions; in meditation many practitioners watch seeing, hearing and thinking arise and pass with their objects.

segments.voice: Yesterday: shaking the palace, and your line, shake the palace. Did one small tap wake you from a bit of pride? Day four hundred thirty-three.

Most of us carry a quiet picture of ourselves: somewhere behind the eyes, a little someone who watches, listens and remembers, the same one at five and at fifty. A monk named Sati, a fisherman's son, carried that picture too, and he was sure the Buddha taught it. As I understand the teaching, he told the other monks, it's this same consciousness that runs on and wanders through birth after birth, not another one. The other monks tried to talk him out of it. He wouldn't budge. Today: Sati's mistake.
screen: `A LITTLE SOMEONE BEHIND THE EYES.` → `SATI, A FISHERMAN'S SON.` → `THE SAME CONSCIOUSNESS, WANDERING ON.`

segments.voice: This is the thirty-eighth discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings, the greater discourse on the ending of craving. The monks bring Sati to the Buddha. Is it true you hold this view? It is, Sati says. What is this consciousness, then? It's what speaks and feels, Sati answers, and experiences the results of good and bad deeds here and there. The Buddha's reply is blunt. He calls Sati a misguided man and asks: to whom have you ever heard me teach it that way? Haven't I said many times that consciousness arises from conditions, and without a condition, there's no consciousness at all? Then he gives a picture. A fire is named by what it burns. A fire burning logs is a log fire. Burning grass, a grass fire. Burning dung, a dung fire. There's no fire apart from its fuel. Consciousness is named the same way. Arising because of the eye and a sight, it's eye-consciousness. Because of the ear and a sound, ear-consciousness. Because of the mind and a thought, mind-consciousness. No little someone sits behind the eyes, waiting, unchanged. Each moment of knowing is lit by what it's knowing. Buddhist schools later worked this out in different ways, including how continuity carries from life to life, but they keep the Buddha's point: consciousness isn't a thing that travels. It's a process that arises. Sati's mistake is easy to make. It's the picture most of us start with. The Buddha didn't replace it with nothing. He replaced it with fire.
screen: `SATI: THE SAME CONSCIOUSNESS GOES ON` · `WITHOUT A CONDITION, NO CONSCIOUSNESS` · `A FIRE IS NAMED BY ITS FUEL` · `EYE AND SIGHT: EYE-CONSCIOUSNESS` · then, large: `FROM CONDITIONS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch hearing arise from sound. Close your eyes, and listen. Wait for a sound: a car, a fan, a bird, your own breath. Notice that hearing doesn't happen before the sound. It lights up with it, like a fire catching on dry grass. When the sound fades, notice hearing that sound fades too. Then wait for the next one. Let each sound make its own small fire of hearing. The bell holds the time.
Sati's mistake. Taking consciousness for one unchanging traveler, when the Buddha taught it arises from conditions, like fire from its fuel. Today's word.
Your line: from conditions. Today, when a strong mood shows up, ask what it's burning: what sight, sound or thought lit it. Day four hundred thirty-three.

match.prompt: fire and its fuel — tap the pairs.

myth: the Buddha agreed that one consciousness wanders unchanged from life to life
he rebuked Sati: he had always taught that consciousness arises from conditions.
in the simile, a fire is named by what it burns
log fire, grass fire, dung fire; consciousness is named by eye, ear, mind and their objects.
Sati was a fisherman's son
the text names him Sati, son of a fisherman.

fork.setup: you're one of the monks. Sati keeps insisting the Buddha taught that the same consciousness wanders on. you've tried to talk him out of it. what do you do next?
options: let him teach it; maybe he's right.
take it to the Buddha.
stop speaking to him.
fork.reveal: the monks bring the matter to the Buddha, who asks Sati directly and then teaches the fire simile to the whole community.

original.note: Pali vinnana: consciousness, the knowing that arises with eye, ear, nose, tongue, body or mind.

trapdoor: what you thought: consciousness is the little someone behind the eyes who stays the same.
what it means: consciousness arises from conditions, like fire from fuel, and is named by what it arises from.
what a scholar hears: MN 38 names six kinds of consciousness by their bases (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind), then goes on to teach dependent origination forward and in reverse.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 38, Mahatanhasankhaya Sutta (the greater discourse on the destruction of craving), opening section

434.title: A life by conditions
434.hook: from conception to awakening, a whole life traced by causes
434.howItsDone: Buddhists learn dependent origination (paticca samuppada) as a chain of conditions, often pictured as a wheel in Tibetan temple art; MN 38 gives it as a human life, from conception and childhood to the release that comes when craving ends.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sati's mistake, and your line, from conditions. Did you catch one mood and see what it was burning? Today, the end of a week, and the same discourse, zoomed all the way out. Day four hundred thirty-four.

Baby photos are strange things. There you are, a few days old, red-faced and furious, and somehow that's you. Then a kid on a tricycle. Then a teenager with that haircut. Everyone who sees the album asks the same question without saying it: how did that one become this one? Near the end of yesterday's discourse, the Buddha answers it. He walks through an entire human life, from before birth to freedom, and shows each step resting on the one before. Today: a life by conditions.
screen: `A BABY PHOTO. A TRICYCLE. THAT HAIRCUT.` → `HOW DID THAT ONE BECOME THIS ONE?` → `A WHOLE LIFE, STEP BY STEP.`

segments.voice: This is the second half of the thirty-eighth discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings. It begins before birth. A life begins, the text says, when three things come together: the mother and father unite, the mother is in season, and a being to be born is present. Not one condition, three. Then the mother carries the child nine or ten months, with great anxiety, and nourishes it after birth with her own milk. The discourse says that in this teaching, mother's milk is called blood. Then the child grows, and the text lists children's games: toy plows, little carts, bows and arrows, somersaults, a game with sticks. Then the adult, enjoying the five kinds of sense pleasure. Seeing a pleasant sight, they lean toward it. An unpleasant one, they lean away. Feeling becomes delight, delight becomes clinging, clinging becomes being, and on rolls the wheel of birth, aging and death. Then the turn. A Buddha appears in the world. The person hears the teaching, gains trust, and trains: virtue, guarding the senses, mindfulness, stillness. Now, seeing a sight, they don't lean. Feeling arises, and no delight hooks it. Without delight, no clinging. Without clinging, the wheel stops. Every stage, the baby, the child, the craving adult and the free one, comes from conditions. That's the hope in it. If the knot was tied by causes, it can be untied by causes. Look back at the week: a grove lit many ways, a cowherd's craft, a debater's sweat, a childhood tree, a trembling palace, a fire and its fuel. All of it, from conditions.
screen: `THREE THINGS, AND A LIFE BEGINS` · `CHILDHOOD GAMES, THEN SENSE PLEASURE` · `FEELING, DELIGHT, CLINGING, BIRTH` · `THE TURN: NO DELIGHT, NO CLINGING` · then, large: `ALL FROM CONDITIONS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: trace one life event's causes. Pick something real that happened to you: a move, a friendship, a job, a loss. Sit, and ask what made it possible. Not one cause: look for three or four. A person you met. A choice you made. Something that happened before you were born. Let each condition appear, and see how none of them alone was enough. Then let it all settle back into the breath, itself coming from conditions. The bell holds the time.
A life by conditions. From conception to childhood, craving and freedom, every stage resting on causes, so every knot can be untied. Today's word.
Your line: all from conditions. Today, when someone frustrates you, remember they too were a baby with games and hungers, shaped by causes. Day four hundred thirty-four.

myth: the discourse says a life begins from one single cause
it names three things that must come together, and each later stage rests on others.
MN 38 lists children's games like toy plows and somersaults
the Buddha walks through childhood in ordinary detail before reaching the adult and craving.
in the discourse, the wheel stops when feeling stops
feeling still arises; it stops when no delight hooks the feeling, so clinging doesn't follow.

fork.setup: you've heard the teaching and trained. you see a beautiful sight, and a pleasant feeling arises. according to MN 38, what happens next for the trained one?
options: delight, then clinging, as always.
the feeling arises, but no delight hooks it.
nothing: they no longer see sights.
fork.reveal: the trained one still sees and feels. what changes is that delight doesn't seize the feeling, and without delight there's no clinging.

original.note: Pali paticca samuppada: dependent origination, things arising by way of conditions.

trapdoor: what you thought: a life is one long thing that just happens to you.
what it means: each stage rests on conditions, which is why the knot of craving can be untied.
what a scholar hears: MN 38 frames the whole life story inside dependent origination, and the discourse's title, the destruction of craving, names what breaks the chain.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 38, Mahatanhasankhaya Sutta (the greater discourse on the destruction of craving), later section
